item.title: Singapore's economy grew 6.1% year on year in the third quarter, above the 5.4% advance estimate, and the ministry raised its 2026 growth forecast to about 6% from 4.5% to 5.5%, citing strong AI-related demand.
item.description:
Singapore's economy grew 6.1% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, above the official advance estimate of 5.4% and the 5.6% expected by economists polled by Reuters, MarketScreener reports; growth eased from 6.4% in the second quarter, according to CNA, a figure The Straits Times describes as revised. On a quarter-on-quarter, seasonally adjusted basis, GDP grew 1.5%. On 24 November the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) raised its 2026 growth forecast to about 6%, from a range of 4.5% to 5.5%, and expects 2027 growth of 2.5% to 4.5%, as growth in most key trading partners is projected to soften and the pace of expansion in new AI investment slows, CNA reports. Strong AI-related demand boosted the machinery, equipment and supplies segment of wholesale trade and the electronics and precision engineering clusters of manufacturing, while retail trade and food and beverage services contracted, according to CNA. Enterprise Singapore raised its 2026 forecast for non-oil domestic exports to growth of 30% to 32%, from 14% to 16%, MarketScreener reports. Factory output rose 3.4% year on year in September, after 15.4% in August, The Straits Times reports.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures show AI-related demand driving Singapore's manufacturing and trade through the third quarter, with an official outlook for slower growth in 2027 as new AI investment grows more slowly. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, Singapore's manufacturing is concentrated in electronics and precision engineering, so its data give an early reading on AI hardware demand in Asian supply chains. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the data point to strong AI-related electronics demand into the third quarter, although factory output growth slowed to 3.4% in September, while the ministry's 2027 range shows the expected slowdown. Points that may be worth considering include whether other Asian electronics exporters revise their 2027 outlooks in the same direction.

MarketScreener | CNA | MarketScreener | The Straits Times

item.title: China's industry ministry has issued a 2026–2030 industrial carbon "dual-control" plan that aims by 2030 for about 400 carbon footprint rules and standards for key industrial products and over 17% less CO2 per unit of industrial value added than in 2025.
item.description:
China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) has recently issued an "Implementation Plan for Accelerating the Construction of a Dual Control System for Carbon Emissions in the Industrial and Information Technology Sector (2026–2030)", China Economic Net reports. By 2030, approximately 400 rules and standards for the carbon footprint accounting of key industrial products are to be formulated and implemented, and around 500 national zero-carbon factories and zero-carbon computing facilities are to be built. Carbon dioxide emissions per unit of value added of industrial enterprises above designated size are to be reduced by more than 17% compared with 2025, and energy consumption per unit of value added by more than 10%. The report does not give the date of issue, name the products the footprint standards will cover, describe how the targets will be enforced, or say whether the plan sets limits on total emissions.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The plan sets 2030 targets for Chinese industry and a programme of product carbon-footprint standards. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, "dual control" in Chinese policy usually refers to controlling both the total amount and the intensity of emissions, and "enterprises above designated size" are the larger industrial firms covered by official statistics; product footprint standards set how the emissions of a product are counted, which customers and regulators can then compare. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, chemical products and the industrial goods they are used in may become subject to common footprint accounting in China, which bears on raw-material and process choices and on the product carbon data customers ask for. Points that may be worth considering include which products the first standards cover and how they relate to footprint rules in the EU.

China Economic Net

item.title: The European Commission proposed a 22nd Russia sanctions package that would cut about 60 Russian banks from SWIFT and extend the energy-services ban to electricity services and to work on refineries, with the 27 EU governments still to decide.
item.description:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a proposal for a 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, which the 27 EU governments will then have to decide on, Il Sole 24 Ore reports; China Economic Net dates the announcement to 23 November in Strasbourg. The transaction ban would be extended to some 60 Russian banks, which would all be removed from the SWIFT payment system, and cryptocurrency platforms would be targeted, Anadolu Agency reports. In energy, the Commission plans to expand the ban on energy services, prohibiting European companies from helping Russia to build, operate or maintain energy infrastructure, particularly refineries, and to include electricity services for the first time, China Economic Net reports. According to China Economic Net, the package would add more than 70 vessels to the so-called Russian "shadow fleet" sanctions list, would ban all oil tankers insured in Russia and would bring third countries that help Russia circumvent sanctions into scope. It would also cover sports and culture and tighten visa rules. Von der Leyen said the aim is to keep pressure on Russia to end its war against Ukraine. The rows do not give a date for the governments' decision or say which governments might object.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The proposal targets Russia's financing, its refining and electricity sectors and its oil shipping through tankers insured in Russia and the so-called shadow fleet; it is not yet adopted. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, measures aimed at refineries and tanker insurance work through oil and refined-product markets, while the bank exclusions mainly affect payments for any remaining trade with Russia. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the direct reach is limited: the package matters mainly through energy and refined-product prices and through compliance checks for European companies with business connected to Russia. Points that may be worth considering include whether all 27 governments approve the package and in what form, and whether the tanker insurance ban changes Russian oil export flows.

Il Sole 24 Ore | Anadolu Agency | China Economic Net

item.title: US rules require contract manufacturers to get export licences for orders from China, Frankfurter Rundschau reports, and Samsung and TSMC have reportedly told Chinese customers they must suspend deliveries while they apply.
item.description:
The US Department of Commerce has issued new regulations requiring contract manufacturers to obtain export licences for orders from China, which has resulted in delivery delays, Frankfurter Rundschau reports. Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which dominate the market for contract semiconductor manufacturing, have reportedly informed their Chinese customers that they must suspend deliveries while they apply for export licences from the US government. The report does not give the date on which the regulation was issued or takes effect, which products or technology levels it covers, how long licence decisions take, how many Chinese customers are affected, or whether licences are expected to be granted. Separately, on 23 November the US added Singapore-based chipmaker Megaspeed to its trade restriction list, Valor Econômico reports; Megaspeed has been investigated by US authorities since 2024 for possible export-control violations related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, and the company says it conducted legal business.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reported rule places the licence requirement on contract manufacturers for orders from China, and the reported suspension applies while licences are pending. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, if the requirement applies across products at the manufacturing stage, it could reach Chinese chip designers that rely on these foundries, not only named companies or products, and a pause of uncertain length can cause supply gaps further down the electronics chain. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, chip packaging and electronics assembly in China depend on chip supply, so a lasting delivery gap could slow parts of Chinese electronics production and shift demand towards domestic Chinese foundries. Points that may be worth considering include the detailed scope of the rule, how quickly licences are granted, and how China responds.

Frankfurter Rundschau | Valor Econômico

item.title: Beijing has released its 2026–2030 urban renewal plan, under which annual urban renewal investment is expected to reach CNY 300 billion, while Guizhou and Wuhan have their own plans and a national plan proposes to accelerate building complete communities.
item.description:
On 23 November the Beijing municipal government released its urban renewal plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period, with 15 main indicators and a series of priority tasks and reform initiatives, Beijing Daily reports. By 2030 the plan aims for important progress and a basically established sustainable renewal model; annual investment in urban renewal is expected to reach CNY 300 billion. China's national 15th Five-Year Plan for urban renewal proposes to accelerate the construction of complete communities and to activate the potential of existing urban resources, China Economic Net reports, quoting General Secretary Xi Jinping that the focus of urban renewal is the improvement of life rather than the expansion of space. Guizhou province's plan includes strengthening the urban underground pipe network, according to China Economic Net, and Wuhan's plan calls for upgrading underused industrial sites, China Daily reports. Urban renewal has risen to a national strategy, with community construction a focal point, Xhby.net reports. The rows give no national investment figure, no split between new building, renovation and infrastructure, and no comparison with spending in the previous five-year period.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The plans set the direction of urban renewal in China and in Beijing, Guizhou and Wuhan for 2026–2030, and only Beijing gives an investment figure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, urban renewal moves construction activity from new districts towards the renovation of existing buildings, communities and pipe networks, and a planned investment figure is a target rather than measured spending. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, renovation work uses sealants, flooring and tile adhesives and waterproofing in existing buildings, so the plans indicate where part of Chinese construction demand may come from in the coming years. Points that may be worth considering include whether other large cities publish investment figures, how much of the planned investment is building work rather than land and services, and how actual spending compares with the expected CNY 300 billion a year.

Beijing Daily | China Economic Net | China Economic Net | China Daily | Xhby.net

item.title: Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Super Micro are seeking price rises of 25% to 45% on some AI server orders that are already signed, citing soaring memory costs and circuit board shortages, Cnyes reports, citing foreign media.
item.description:
Manufacturers including Dell, Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), Lenovo and Super Micro are demanding higher prices from customers for AI server orders that have already been signed, with some orders seeing price increases of 25% to 45%, Cnyes reports, citing the latest foreign media reports. These servers typically contain Nvidia or AMD GPUs, memory chips and networking equipment. The suppliers cite soaring memory costs and circuit board shortages. According to JPMorgan Chase research, memory prices have risen by more than 400% cumulatively since early 2024, and server DRAM contract prices alone rose by about 90% in the first quarter of this year. HPE's chief executive Antonio Neri said memory prices now exceed half of the material cost of a server. Affected customers include the quantitative trading firms Jane Street, Optiver and Hudson River Trading, which are building large data centres. The report does not say how many orders are affected, whether customers have accepted the increases, or whether large cloud providers face the same demands.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The report describes server makers passing component costs through to customers on contracts already signed; it describes prices, not the number of servers bought. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, GPUs are the graphics processors used for AI computing and DRAM is the main working memory, and re-pricing signed orders is unusual and suggests suppliers cannot absorb the cost increase. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, data centres and electronics are among the growth markets named in the Adhesive and Sealant Council survey in this alert; higher server costs could delay some data-centre projects at the margin, while memory and circuit board shortages point to tight capacity in electronics manufacturing, where bonding, encapsulation and thermal materials are used. Points that may be worth considering include whether customers accept or cancel the re-priced orders and how memory prices develop.

Cnyes

item.title: Germany's composite purchasing managers' index rose to 55 points in November from 53.4 in October, the highest in more than four and a half years, while the eurozone index was unchanged at 51.7 in a preliminary estimate and France weakened.
item.description:
The S&P Global composite purchasing managers' index (PMI) for Germany rose from 53.4 points in October to 55 in November, its highest level in more than four and a half years, Handelsblatt reports; economists had expected a decline to 53.2. The 50-point mark separates growth from contraction. In Germany, sentiment in both industrial companies and the services sector improved unexpectedly, with both indicators well above the growth threshold, WirtschaftsWoche reports. For the eurozone as a whole, the index stayed at 51.7 in November according to a preliminary estimate, against an expected 52.0. S&P Global Market Intelligence's chief economist Chris Williamson described a "stable upward trend" but "worrying differences at the country level". In France, both indicators point to weakening, with sentiment in industrial companies deteriorating significantly further, according to WirtschaftsWoche. Handelsblatt attributes Germany's recovery course to government investment and increasing export demand, and France's downturn to political uncertainty, concerns about public finances and the upcoming elections. The cited reports do not give separate manufacturing and services readings for Germany, nor the new-orders or price components of the survey.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reading is a survey of purchasing managers that shows a broad improvement in German business activity in November, in industry as well as services, against a flat eurozone and a weaker France. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a purchasing managers' index measures how many companies report growth rather than how large the growth is, and one month's reading can be revised. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, an upturn in Germany driven by government investment and export demand can reach industrial and construction-related demand in the home market with a delay, while a flat eurozone average hides home markets that move in opposite directions. Points that may be worth considering include whether the December reading confirms the rise, and whether government investment shows up in German industrial and construction orders.

Handelsblatt | WirtschaftsWoche

item.title: German carmakers and suppliers including Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Bosch and Schaeffler plan job cuts and possible plant closures, and four German factories currently have no successor vehicle models planned, LiveMint reports.
item.description:
Germany's carmakers face months of contentious labour talks and strikes over job cuts and potential plant closures, MarketScreener reports. Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Bosch and Schaeffler have responded to Chinese competition, US tariffs and weaker demand with plans to cut thousands of jobs, curb investment and potentially close plants, MarketScreener reports. China Daily, which cites US tariffs, the shift to electric vehicles and weaker demand, says they are moving to cut thousands of jobs and trim investment and are considering shutting sites. LiveMint also names BMW among the carmakers preparing cost-cutting measures. China Daily reports that in October Volkswagen posted its biggest operating loss in more than a decade, and that Mercedes-Benz's and BMW's nine-month auto margins fell to 1.9% and 3.5%, from 14.9% and 8.7% four years earlier. According to LiveMint, Volkswagen is working towards a restructuring plan for its European manufacturing operations by June 2027, four German factories currently have no successor vehicle models planned, and Volkswagen is preparing for fresh talks with IG Metall over proposed salary reductions and job cuts. IG Metall has threatened industrial action at Volkswagen from 1 January if no agreement is reached, China Daily and LiveMint report. LiveMint adds that workers at Porsche and Mercedes-Benz staged warning strikes as part of a broader regional industrial action organised by IG Metall. The rows do not name the four plants, give a total for planned job cuts, or give production volumes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reported measures combine falling profitability at the premium carmakers (nine-month margins, not volumes) with plans that reach German production capacity: plants without successor models, a European restructuring plan that Volkswagen is working to finalise by June 2027 and a strike threat at Volkswagen from 1 January. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a plant without a successor model loses its production volume when the current model ends, so the effect on German vehicle output comes over several years rather than at once, while a strike would interrupt output only for its duration. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the question for suppliers to German vehicle production is where future models will be built rather than this quarter's volume, and margins at these levels usually mean continued pressure on purchase prices. Points that may be worth considering include which plants Volkswagen's restructuring plan affects, where successor models are allocated, and whether the 1 January strike threat is carried out.

China Daily | LiveMint | MarketScreener

item.title: A Bain & Company report says the chemical industry would need to close about 7.5% of global olefin capacity by 2030 to return to normal operating rates, as some cuts in Europe, Korea and Japan do not offset the pace of China's additions.
item.description:
According to a report from Bain & Company, reported by the Society of Chemical Industry (SCI), the global chemical industry would need to collectively shut about 7.5% of global olefin production capacity by 2030, equivalent to 35 million metric tons, if it wants to return to normal operating rates. While some capacity is being cut in Europe, Korea and Japan, it is not enough to offset the pace of China's capacity additions, Bain says. The price rises for chemicals following the Iran conflict have opened a temporary window for companies to reset their strategies, according to the report, and companies that mistake this temporary boost for a recovery risk missing the opportunity to act. Bain says decisions on closing or converting high-cost, carbon-exposed assets should be made within the next 12 to 18 months, while the window remains open. The report as summarised does not give current operating rates, the capacity already announced for closure by region, the level of the price rises, or which assets Bain regards as high-cost.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Bain's figure is an estimate of what would be needed, not a plan, and the 12 to 18 month window is the consultancy's view. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, olefins such as ethylene and propylene are the basic petrochemicals from which most plastics and many polymers are made, so closures on this scale would change where the start of the polymer chain is produced. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, polymers and resins derived from olefins are a large part of raw-material cost, and closures concentrated outside China would make supply more dependent on Chinese capacity, while the Iran-related price rise is temporary on Bain's account. Points that may be worth considering include which crackers in Europe and Asia are announced for closure or conversion, how regional supply of polymer raw materials changes, and whether chemical prices fall back as the Iran-related effect fades.

SCI

item.title: In the Adhesive and Sealant Council's Q3 survey, 82% of North American adhesives and sealants companies reported higher revenue than a year earlier, up from 79% in Q2, while the share reporting higher shipments fell to 66% from 74%.
item.description:
The Adhesive and Sealant Council's (ASC) Q3 2026 Industry Pulse Survey covers companies in the North American adhesives and sealants industry. 82% reported higher revenue in the third quarter than in the same quarter of 2025, up from 79% in the second quarter and 61% in the first. 72% reported higher profits, up from 69% and 57%. 66% reported higher shipments, down 8 points from 74% in the second quarter but above the 50% of the first quarter, and only 30% reported adding headcount, the lowest share of the year, against 37% in the second quarter and 35% in the first. Respondents described growth that is concentrated in a few end markets: data centres, electronics and computers, defence and aerospace, and new automotive and security business. Many other segments were described as flat or growing at low single digits. Building and construction, particularly housing, was repeatedly named as stalled, with high interest and mortgage rates and weaker consumer purchasing power holding back new construction and renovation. Looking ahead, 82% of companies expect revenue to grow over the next 12 months, down from 90% in the second quarter and 89% in the first. The summary reports shares of companies, not totals, and does not give the number of respondents, the size of the revenue or shipment changes, or prices.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is the industry's own quarterly reading for North America, and it shows broad revenue growth together with a narrower base of shipment growth, slower hiring and a cooler outlook, with construction and housing named as stalled. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, when more companies report higher revenue than higher shipments, part of the revenue growth is likely to come from price or product mix rather than from volume. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the survey points to North American demand concentrated in data centres, electronics, defence and aerospace and new automotive business, while construction-related demand waits on lower interest rates. Points that may be worth considering include whether the shipments share falls again in the fourth quarter, whether the end markets named as growing are the ones that also drive volume, and how the lower share of companies expecting growth compares with order intake.

Adhesive and Sealant Council
